# Instruction Set Architecture

This chapter describes the MISA instruction set architecture, including the base instruction set,
optional assembler extensions, special registers and hardware data structures, and other
implementation-agnostic features.

The MISA architecture is an 8-bit architecture with up to a 16-bit address bus to interface with
externally connected memory. Instructions are fixed-width 16-bit doublewords in little-endian byte
order.

The information presented in this chapter is referred to as the MISA core architecture. The last
section of this chapter enumerates several optional extensions to the core architecture, although an
implementation is considered conforming if it implements at least the core architecture.

## Conformance Language

For an implementation of the MISA architecture to be considered "conforming" to this chapter, there
are several requirements it needs to respect, although some liberty is given to the implementation.

The following words used in this chapter have specific meanings when describing whether and how a
conforming implementation implements a part of the architecture:

- "MUST": A conforming implementation is required to include or omit the specified feature/behavior.
  If the implementation does not respect the requirement, it is not considered conforming to this
  specification.
- "SHOULD": A conforming implementation can choose whether or not to include the specified feature,
  but this specification recommends its inclusion. Implementations that do not include the feature
  are still considered conforming, but some aspect of the implementation may suffer.
- "MAY": A conforming implementation can choose whether or not to include the specified feature.
  Both an implementation that does, and an implementation that does not include the feature will be
  considered conforming. This specification makes no recommendation on the inclusion of the feature.
  
This normative terminology will appear in ALL CAPS throughout this chapter.

## General Purpose Registers

The general-purpose register file MUST contain sixteen, 8-bit registers for general computation and
data storage, defined by the following ABI:

| ABI Name | ABI Purpose | Wide ABI Name | Encoding |
|-------------|---------------------------|---------------|----------|
| `R0` | Hard-wired zero | N/A | 0000 |
| `RA` | Argument/temporary | `RAB` | 0001 |
| `RB` | Argument/temporary | | 0010 |
| `RC` | Argument/temporary | `RCD` | 0011 |
| `RD` | Argument/temporary | | 0100 |
| `RE` | Argument/temporary | `REF` | 0101 |
| `RF` | Argument/temporary | | 0110 |
| `RU` | Saved | `RUV` | 0111 |
| `RV` | Saved | | 1000 |
| `RW` | Saved | `RWX` | 1001 |
| `RX` | Saved | | 1010 |
| `RY` | Saved | `RYZ` | 1011 |
| `RZ` | Saved | | 1100 |
| `RT` | Argument/return/temporary | N/A | 1101 |
| `RSCRATCH0` | Assembler scratch | `RSCRATCH` | 1110 |
| `RSCRATCH1` | Assembler scratch | | 1111 |

The `R0` register MUST be hard-wired to ignore writes and always return the value `0b00000000` on
reads. Wide registers are formed by two general-purpose registers, which MUST be equivalent to using
the two 8-bit register names in order. For instance, `RAB` MUST be semantically equivalent to `RA,
RB` in that order. General purpose registers are taken as the operands to most instructions which
operate on registers.

Argument and return registers SHOULD be `RA` - `RF` and `RT`. The `RT` register SHOULD be used as
the first return register, if the value being returned logically fits in a single (not wide)
register.  Otherwise, the register pair `RAB` SHOULD be preferred as the first return
register. Argument registers SHOULD also be usable as temporary registers (caller-saved). `RU`
through `RZ` SHOULD be saved registers (callee-saved).

The `RSCRATCH` wide register SHOULD be reserved as a "scratch" 16-bit register for the
assembler. Certain pseudo-instructions and other macros MAY use this register when a temporary value
is needed (like loading an address to jump to). As such, the value of `RSCRATCH` SHOULD not be
assumed to persist over time.

## Control and Status Registers

A few special registers MUST also be supported, which cannot be used as instruction operands, but
can be read and written from general purpose registers with the `RSR` and `WSR`
instructions. Special registers are generally wider 16-bit registers that are required for the
operation of certain instructions.

When used as operands for instructions, the special registers are encoded as follows:

| ABI Name | Encoding |
|----------|------------------------------------|
| `SADDR` | 0001 |
| `RADDR` | 0010 |
| `FLAGS` | 0011 |
| `CAUSE` | 0100 |
| `EXTNS` | 0101 |
| `RETSC` | 1000 (under System Call Extension) |
| `RETIR` | 1001 (under Interrupt Extension) |
| `PRIVS` | 1010 (under Privilege Extension) |

The following sub-sections describe the purpose and layout of each special register.

### `SADDR`

The stack address or stack pointer. `SADDR` MUST be at least an 8-bit register (supporting stack
addresses `0x00` - `0xFF` with a possible high 8-bit prefix) and MUST not be more than a 16-bit
register.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "SADDR LO (required)", "bits": 8},
        {"name": "SADDR HI (optional)", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `RADDR`

The return address. `RADDR` MUST be wide enough to store an absolute address for the connected
memory, which SHOULD be 16-bit.

The return address special register is not used by specific base instructions, but provides a
dedicated 16-bit-wide register for subroutine calling. The `JAL` instruction MUST set the `RADDR`
register with the address of the instruction after the `JAL`. Returning to the location in `RADDR`
can be done with a `RSR` and `JMP` or a `JMP` using `RADDR` as the branch target.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RADDR", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `FLAGS`

Conditional branching in the MISA architecture is based on ALU flag values for comparing integers.
Both branching instructions, `JAL` and `JMP`, MUST these flags to make decisions on whether a branch
will be taken.

`FLAGS` MUST be set based on the result of each ALU operation. The instructions which MUST update
the `FLAGS` register are: `ADD`, `ADC`, `SUB`, `SBB`, `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `RRC`. Instructions which
MUST NOT update the `FLAGS` register are: `HALT`, `SET`, `LD`, `ST`, `RSR`, `WSR` (MUST NOT update
`FLAGS` asynchronously through the ALU output, but MUST update `FLAGS` if writing directly to it),
`JAL`, `JMP`. A conditional branch that relies on `FLAGS` SHOULD be performed immediately after the
conditional comparison or a `WSR` to `FLAGS`.

The `FLAGS` special register is a flags register (one bit per flag) which MUST be at least 4 bits
and support the following:

| Flag | Bit | Commentary |
|------|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Z` | 0 | Whether the last ALU operation's output was zero.  |
| `C` | 1 | The adder carry out bit of the last ALU operation.  |
| `N` | 2 | Whether the last ALU operation's output was negative (MSB = 1).  |
| `V` | 3 | Whether the last ALU operation's output overflowed (sign inversion). |

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "Z", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "C", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "N", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "V", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "Reserved (optional)", "bits": 12}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The `FLAGS` register can be accessed indirectly with the conditional jump instructions using special
assembler symbols:

| ABI Name | Logical Meaning | Encoding |
|-----------------|------------------|----------|
| `ALWAYS` | `1` | 000 |
| `EQUAL` | `Z` | 001 |
| `NOT_EQUAL` | `~Z` | 010 |
| `GREATER` | `~((N ^ V) | Z)` | 011 |
| `LESS` | `N ^ V` | 100 |
| `GREATER_EQUAL` | `~(N ^ V)` | 101 |
| `LESS_EQUAL` | `(N ^ V) | Z` | 110 |

These comparison flags, when passed as a conditional branch instruction operand, MUST perform the
specified boolean logic on the fields of the `FLAGS` register. If the result is `1`, the branch is
taken, otherwise the branch is not taken. The assumption is that a comparison of registers `RS1` and
`RS2` is performed by invoking `SUB R0 RS1 RS2`, which sets the ALU flags appropriately for deciding
`RS1 ? RS2` where `?` is a comparison operator.

### `CAUSE`

The `CAUSE` special register holds information about the status of the processor during exceptions,
faults, and termination. It MUST be set when the `HALT` instruction is executed, when syscalls are
made under the System Call Extension, and when fault behavior (such as a malformed instruction
decode) occurs during execution.

`CAUSE` is a 16-bit register with the following fields:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "Reason", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Type", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Reserved", "bits": 2},
        {"name": "Extended status", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

| Reason | Encoding |
|-------------------|----------|
| None | 000 |
| Instruction usage | 001 |
| Memory usage | 010 |
| Control event | 011 |

#### `CAUSE` Reason: None
The `CAUSE` register does not represent an exception, or represents an unknown/generic exception
without a reason. If the reason is 000, the Type and Extended status fields have no significance.

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Instruction Usage
The exception cause is related to the use of a specific instruction or class of instructions. The
valid Type fields are:

| Type | Encoding | Commentary |
|------------------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Halt instruction | 000 | The `HALT` instruction was executed. Extended status is the value of the `RS` operand register. Under the System Call Extension, this reason indicates that the `SYSCALL` instruction was executed. |
| Illegal instruction | 001 | An ill-formed instruction failed to decode. Extended status is not used.  |
| Privileged instruction | 010 | A privileged instruction was executed while in User Mode (under Privilege Extension).  |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Memory Usage
The exception cause is related to the use of an address or memory operation. The valid Type fields
are:

| Type | Encoding | Commentary |
|-------------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Address overflow | 000 | A memory operation attempted to access an address which is outside the mapped memory space.  |
| PC overflow | 001 | The program counter overflowed an unsigned 16-bit value.  |
| Privileged access | 010 | An access to privileged memory was attempted while in User Mode (under Privilege Extension). |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Control Event
The exception cause is related to an exception or interrupt control flow event. The valid Type
fields are:

| Type | Encoding | Commentary |
|----------------------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Improper return context | 000 | Either: `JMP ALWAYS RETSC` was executed outside of a system call context or inside of an interrupt context; `JMP ALWAYS RETIR` was executed outside of an interrupt context. The extended status is set as follows: bit 0 = in system call context, bit 1 = in interrupt context, bits 2-3 = reserved, bits 4-7 = `JMP` target CSR register index. |
| Conditional context return | 001 | `JMP` was executed with a branch target of `RETSC` or `RETIR` but a comparison other than `ALWAYS`. The extended status is set as follows: bits 0-2 = comparison type, bit 3 = reserved, bits 4-7 = `JMP` target CSR register index.  |
| Improper system call | 010 | A system call was executed while the processor was in a system call or interrupt context. The extended status is set as follows: bit 0 = in system call context, bit 1 = in interrupt context.  |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

### `EXTNS`

The `EXTNS` special register is a flags register that holds information about which (if any)
architectural extensions are supported by the hardware. All implementations of the MISA architecture
MUST include the `EXTNS` register, even those which only implement the core architecture. A
core-only implementation can be identified by `EXTNS == 0x0000`.

Unlike most special registers, writes to `EXTNS` MAY be ignored (i.e. the register MAY have a
hard-coded value). For more information on writes to `EXTNS`, see the Dynamic Hardware Extension.
Note that bit 0 (the Dynamic Hardware Extension) MUST ignore writes regardless of its state,
preventing the Dynamic Hardware Extension from disabling itself.

`EXTNS` MUST support at least the following bits:

| Bit | Extension |
|-----|----------------------------|
| 0 | Dynamic Hardware Extension |
| 1 | System Call Extension |
| 2 | Privilege Extension |
| 3 | Interrupt Extension |

## Data Formats and Alignments

The MISA architecture defined in this chapter only supports 8-bit signed integers using two's
complement encoding, where the value of an integer is given by the sum of its active bits:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "1", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "2", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "4", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "8", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "16", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "32", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "64", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "-128", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 8}
})).tostring())
```

16-bit data types MAY be supported in software using the `ADC` and `SBB` instructions for
arithmetic.

## Memory

The MISA architecture MAY support up to a 16-bit address bus for memory operations, and memory MUST
be byte-addressable. While the memory map for applications using the MISA architecture is generally
free for the user to decide, this section will cover both a recommended map and specific regions
which are required by all maps.

### Required Memory Regions

The region 0xFFF0 - 0xFFFF MUST be reserved for a reset vector table. When the processor is taken
out of reset, the program counter MUST be initialized to the address stored in memory at 0xFFFE -
0xFFFF and begin execution there.

The reset vector table contains the following function pointers:

| Vector Address | Purpose |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `0xFFF0 - 0xFFF1` | Reserved |
| `0xFFF2 - 0xFFF3` | Reserved |
| `0xFFF4 - 0xFFF5` | Reserved |
| `0xFFF6 - 0xFFF7` | Reserved |
| `0xFFF8 - 0xFFF9` | Interrupt handler (under Interrupt Extension) |
| `0xFFFA - 0xFFFB` | Syscall handler (under System Call Extension) |
| `0xFFFC - 0xFFFD` | Fault handler |
| `0xFFFE - 0xFFFF` | Reset handler |

### Recommended Memory Map

The linker script recommended by default is as follows:
```
// Zero page, which may have fast access on some hardware
SECTION 0x0000 - 0x00FF : direct ;

// Stack, SADDR initialized to 0x(01)FF and decrements
SECTION 0x0100 - 0x01FF : ;

// RAM, may support software-implemented stack or heap
SECTION 0x0200 - 0x7FFF : data bss ;

// Memory-mapped IO and IO buffers
SECTION 0x8000 - 0xBFFF : ;

// Program ROM
SECTION 0xC000 - 0xFFEF : text rodata ;

// Vector table
SECTION 0xFFF0 - 0xFFFF : vectors ;
```

Which defines the following sections by convention:

| Section | Commentary |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `direct` | Contents to place in the first 256-byte page. This page may support faster memory operations on certain hardware implementations, and thus may be a desirable target for frequently accessed data. |
| `data` | Initialized global data that is mutable.  |
| `bss` | Declared but uninitialized global data that is mutable. Runtime/startup code should initialize `bss` symbols to zero.  |
| `text` | Executable and immutable program code.  |
| `rodata` | Initialized global constants.  |
| `vectors` | A small region for reset vector function addresses.  |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10, 90]"}

### Stack Conventions

The stack SHOULD be towards-lower-address, which grows towards `0x0000` on pushes and contracts
towards `0xFFFF` on pops. This convention SHOULD be respected regardless of the supported width of
the `SADDR` special register or the location in memory of the stack.

Stack operations SHOULD respect the convention of the `PUSH` and `POP` assembler macros. That is,
pushing to the stack SHOULD write before decrementing `SADDR`, and popping from the stack SHOULD
increment `SADDR` before reading.

Multi-byte pushes and pops SHOULD be logically equivalent to chaining several `PUSH` or `POP`
assembler macros.

## Reset

When the processor is taken out of the reset state, some internal state MUST be initialized:

- The reset vector address stored in memory at `0xFFFE - 0xFFFF` MUST be read and used to initialize
  the program counter.

The state of general purpose registers and control and status registers is not defined.

## Faults

Fault conditions occur when something goes wrong during program execution. This includes:

- Bad instruction decodes
- Overflow of the program counter
- Etc.

When a fault is detected, the processor MUST set the `CAUSE` register based on the type of fault and
then set the program counter to the fault vector address stored in memory at `0xFFFC - 0xFFFD`.
Execution MUST then continue in the fault handler, which is software-defined and MAY attempt
recovery, dump diagnostic information, or simply halt.

## Exceptions and Interrupts

The core ISA defined in this chapter does not support traditional exceptions or interrupts. The
`CAUSE` special register is intended for use as a diagnostic tool in the core architecture, and
`HALT` is the only instruction that MUST update it.

A basic synchronous exception system is supported under the System Call Extension which, when
combined with the Privilege Extension, MAY be used to invoke privileged routines from the
unprivileged user mode.

The Interrupt Extension provides support for basic asynchronous interrupts, which MAY be used to let
the processor more easily keep time and interact with peripherals.

## Base Instructions

Sixteen base instructions (with distinct opcodes and behavior) MUST be supported by the MISA
architecture. This is a hard limit, and the 8-bit MISA architecture does not allow for more than 4
bits of opcode in each instruction word. This subsection defines all the base instructions and their
behavior on the microprocessor's state.

Instruction behavior is given under the "Meaning" label, which is a formalism for how the
instruction should affect the behavior of the processor. The following syntax is used when
describing instruction behavior:

- `Register`: The general-purpose register file, indexed by the register number from 0-15
- `Special`: The special register file, indexed by the special register number from 0-15
- `Memory`: The mapped memory, indexed by an address from 0-64K
- `Check`: The truth value from the current state of `FLAGS`, indexed by a comparison operand
- `PC`: The program counter
- `Halt`: Stop processor execution
- `Update`: Update a value using a definition/ruleset provided elsewhere in this chapter
- `If`: Perform the encapsulated operations only if a condition is true

### `HALT`
Usage: `HALT RS`

Description: Halt the processor and emit the contents of `RS` for debug.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0000")],
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Special[CAUSE] = Register[RS] << 8 | 0x01;
Halt;
```

### `ADD`
Usage: `ADD RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Add the content of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0001")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = Register[RS1] + Register[RS2];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `ADC`
Usage: `ADC RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Add the contents of `RS1`, `RS2`, and the `C` field of the `FLAGS` register and store
the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0010")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = Register[RS1] + Register[RS2] + Special[FLAGS.C];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `SUB`
Usage: `SUB RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Subtract the contents of `RS2` from `RS1` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0011")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = Register[RS1] - Register[RS2];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `SBB`
Usage: `SBB RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Add the contents of `RS1`, the bitwise complement of `RS2`, and the `C` field of the
`FLAGS` register, and store the result in `RD`. Because `C` is the adder carry out, this equals
`RS1 - RS2 - (1 - C)`, so chaining `SUB` then `SBB` subtracts a multi-byte value with the borrow
carried through `C`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0100")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Regsiter[RD] = Register[RS1] + ~Register[RS2] + Special[FLAGS.C];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `AND`
Usage: `AND RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise AND of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result in
`RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0101")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = Register[RS1] & Register[RS2];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `OR`
Usage: `OR RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise OR of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0110")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Regsiter[RD] = Register[RS1] | Register[RS2];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `XOR`
Usage: `XOR RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise exclusive OR of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the
result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0111")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Regsiter[RD] = Register[RS1] ^ Register[RS2];
Update Special[FLAGS];
```

### `RRC`
Usage: `RRC RD RS`

Description: Shift the 9-bit integer formed by `{C, RS}` right by one bit. Store the shifted result
in `RD` and the LSB of `RS` into `C`. The ALU flags are updated from the 8-bit result. `Z` is set
when the result is zero, `N` takes the most significant bit of the result, and `V` is cleared. `C`
receives the shifted-out LSB of `RS` as described above.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1000")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = (Special[FLAGS.C] << 0x07) | (Register[RS] >> 0x01);
Update Special[FLAGS];
Special[FLAGS.C] = Register[RS] & 0x01;
```

### `SET`
Usage: `SET RD IMM`

Description: Store the provided 8-bit immediate value into `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1001")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "IMM", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RD] = IMM;
```

### `LD`
Usage: `LD RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Load the 8-bit word at the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}` into `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1010")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

### `ST`
Usage: `ST RD RS1 RS2`

Description: Store the 8-bit word in `RD` to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1011")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

### `RSR`
Usage: `RSR CSR RS1 RS2`

Description: Read the 16-bit control and status register `CSR` into the two 8-bit general purpose
registers `{RS1, RS2}`

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1100")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Register[RS1] = Special[CSR] >> 0x08;
Register[RS2] = Special[CSR] & 0xFF;
```

### `WSR`
Usage: `WSR CSR RS1 RS2`

Description: Write the contents formed by `{RS1, RS2}` into the 16-bit control and status register
`CSR`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1101")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Special[CSR] = (Register[RS1] << 0x08) | Register[RS2];
```

### `JAL`
Usage: `JAL CMP RS1 RS2`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`RADDR` to the address of the next instruction and set `PC` to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}`.
Note that `JAL` does not support using special registers as a branch target like `JMP` does.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1110")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
If (Check[CMP]) {
  Special[RADDR] = PC + 0x02;
  PC = (Register[RS1] << 0x08) | Register[RS2];
}
```

### `JMP`
`JMP` has two variants depending on the branch target. The most significant bit of the instruction
encoding identifies the target source.

#### General Purpose Register Target
Usage: `JMP CMP RS1 RS2`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set `PC`
to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}`.

Encoding (when the branch target is stored in two general-purpose registers):
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1111")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "0", "bits": 1},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
If (Check[CMP]) {
  PC = (Register[RS1] << 0x08) | Register[RS2];
}
```

#### Special Register Target
Usage: `JMP CMP CSR`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set `PC`
to the address in `CSR`. Jumping to the 16-bit value in a special register is intended to be used
for quickly returning to addresses like `RADDR`, `RETSC`, and `RETIR`.

Encoding (when the branch target is stored in one special register):
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1111")],
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "1", "bits": 1},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
If (Check[CMP]) {
  PC = Special[CSR];
}
```

## Pseudo Instructions

Because of the limitations of the core instruction set, implementations SHOULD additionally provide
the following set of assembler macros whose functionality can be represented by one or more of the
base instructions.

The semantic meaning of pseudo instructions is given in terms of a sequence of base instructions to
be executed in order. Implementations providing pseudo instructions MAY use a different definition,
but the semantic behavior MUST match.

### `ADD2`
Usage: `ADD2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Description: Add the 16-bit values `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store the result in `{RD1,
RD2}`.

Meaning:
```
ADD RD2 RS2 RS4
ADC RD1 RS1 RS3
```

### `AND2`
Usage: `AND2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Description: Compute the bitwise AND of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store the
result in `{RD1, RD2}`

Meaning:
```
AND RD2 RS2 RS4
AND RD1 RS1 RS3
```

### `CALL`
Usage: `CALL IMM`

Description: Jump to the subroutine at the address `IMM` and link with the `RADDR` special register.

Meaning:
```
SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 0x08)
SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)
JAL ALWAYS RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1
```

### `CLR`
Usage: `CLR`

Description: Set the `FLAGS` special register to zero, effectively lowering all flags.

Meaning:
```
WSR FLAGS R0 R0
```

### `CMP`
Usage: `CMP RS1 RS2`

Description: Perform an arithmetic operation which will set the `FLAGS` register such that the
boolean operation `?` can be performed on `RS1 ? RS2`.

Meaning:
```
SUB R0 RS1 RS2
```

### `GOTO`
Usage: `GOTO IMM`

Description: Unconditionally jump to the address `IMM`.

Meaning:
```
SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 0x08)
SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)
JMP ALWAYS RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1
```

### `JALI`
Usage: `JALI CMP IMM`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`RADDR` to the address of the next instruction and set `PC` to the address `IMM`.

Meaning:
```
SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 0x08)
SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)
JAL CMP RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1
```

### `JMPI`
Usage: `JMPI CMP IMM`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set `PC`
to the address `IMM`.

Meaning:
```
SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 0x08)
SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)
JMP CMP RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1
```

### `MOV`
Usage: `MOV RD RS1`

Description: Copy the contents of `RS1` into `RD`.

Meaning:
```
OR RD RS1 R0
```

### `MOV2`
Usage: `MOV2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2`

Description: Copy the contents of the 16-bit value `{RS1, RS2}` into `{RD1, RD2}`.

Meaning:
```
MOV RD2 RS2
MOV RD1 RS1
```

### `NOP`
Usage: `NOP`

Description: Do nothing.

Meaning:
```
SET R0 0x00
```

### `OR2`
Usage: `OR2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Description: Compute the bitwise OR of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store the
result in `{RD1, RD2}`.

Meaning:
```
OR RD2 RS2 RS4
OR RD1 RS1 RS3
```

### `POP`
Usage: `POP RD`

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

Description: Increment `SADDR` by 1 byte and then load the byte at the new stack address into `RD`.

### `POP2`
Usage: `POP2 RD1 RD2`

Description: Pop a 16-bit value off the stack and into `{RD1, RD2}`.

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

### `PUSH`
Usage: `PUSH RS`

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

Description: Write `RS` onto the stack at `SADDR`, and then decrement `SADDR` by 1 byte.

### `PUSH2`
Usage: `PUSH2 RS1 RS2`

Description: Push a 16-bit value onto the stack from `{RS1, RS2}`.

Meaning:
```
MARK
```

### `RET`
Usage: `RET`

Description: Return to the address in `RADDR`.

Meaning:
```
JMP ALWAYS RADDR
```

### `RRC2`
Usage: `RRC2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2`

Description: Shift the 17-bit integer formed by `{C, RS1, RS2}` right by one bit. Store the shifted
result in `{RD1, RD2}` and the LSB of `RS2` into `C`.

Meaning:
```
RRC RD1 RS1
RRC RD2 RS2
```

### `SET2`
Usage: `SET2 RS1 RS2 IMM`

Description: Set both the `RS1` and `RS2` registers from the high and low halves of a 16-bit
immediate value.

Meaning:
```
SET RS1 (IMM >> 0x8)
SET RS2 (IMM & 0xFF)
```

### `SUB2`
Usage: `SUB2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Description: Subtract the 16-bit value `{RS3, RS4}` from `{RS1, RS2}` and store the result in `{RD1,
RD2}`.

Meaning:
```
SUB RD2 RS2 RS4
SBB RD1 RS1 RS3
```

### `XOR2`
Usage: `XOR2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Description: Compute the bitwise XOR of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store the
result in `{RD1, RD2}`

Meaning:
```
XOR RD2 RS2 RS4
XOR RD1 RS1 RS3
```

## Architecture Extensions

The content in this chapter until this point is the MISA core architecture. This section provides a
description of several optional extensions to that architecture which enable additional
functionalities.

### Dynamic Hardware Extension

The Dynamic Hardware Extension enables writes to the `EXTNS` special register and thus dynamic
support for the architecture extensions discussed in this section.

**Note:** If the Dynamic Hardware Extension is supported, writes to the Dynamic Hardware Extension
bit of the `EXTNS` special register MUST always be ignored. The extension cannot be used to disable
itself at runtime.

If the Dynamic Hardware Extension is not supported, writes to any bit of `EXTNS` MUST be
ignored. The list of supported extensions is static and a property of the hardware itself. If
supported, writes MUST take effect on the instruction following the `WSR`.

Partial support of the Dynamic Hardware Extension is also allowed. That is, an implementation MAY
only permit enabling/disabling specific, but not every extension at runtime. In that case, writes to
the bit of any extension that cannot be toggled MUST be ignored. Software should treat the lack of
change in the target bit as a signal that the target extension is permanently enabled/disabled.

### System Call Extension

The System Call Extension extends the `HALT` instruction in the core architecture to support basic
synchronous exceptions that MAY be used for system calls and other similar features.

#### `SYSCALL`
The `SYSCALL` instruction replaces the `HALT` instruction in the assembler under the System Call
Extension. Its usage is similar to `HALT`, but with a conditional "exception" bit that controls the
terminal behavior of the processor.

Usage: `SYSCALL RS`

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0000")],
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 7},
        {"name": "E", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Meaning:
```
Special[CAUSE] = Register[RS] << 8 | 0x01;
If (E == 0b0) {
  Halt;
}
If (E == 0b1) {
  PC = (Memory[0xFFFB] << 0x08) | Memory[0xFFFA];
}
```

#### `HALT`
`HALT` functionality as defined in the core architecture is supported under the System Call
Extension by setting the `E` bit to `0`. Assemblers MUST set `E` to `0` when the `HALT` opcode is
used, and set `E` to `1` when the `SYSCALL` opcode is used.

#### Calling Conventions and Stack Frame
When a `SYSCALL` instruction is executed, the contents of the `RS` register are used as the syscall
code, stored in the `CAUSE` special register. The syscall handler address at `0xFFFA - 0xFFFB` is
responsible for reading the `CAUSE` register, understanding that a syscall was executed, and using
the extended status value to branch to different handler code for each type of call.

General purpose registers follow the same caller-callee conventions as standard subroutine/function
calls in the MISA ABI. This includes which registers are used as arguments to the system call, and
which registers are used as return values from the system call. All special registers MUST be saved
and restored by the system call routine.

#### Nested System Calls
The `SYSCALL` instruction cannot be executed within a system call context. The processor is
canonically in a system call context under the following formal definition:

- The processor enters a system call context when the `SYSCALL` instruction is executed with the
  exception bit set
- The processor leaves the system call context when a `JMP ALWAYS RETSC` instruction is executed
- Every instruction executed between entering and leaving the system call context exists within the
  system call context
  
If a secondary `SYSCALL` is performed in a system call context, a fault MUST occur with the `CAUSE`
Reason "Control event" and the `CAUSE` Type "Improper system call".

#### Returning From System Calls
To return from system calls, the `RETSC` special register is defined, which stores the return
address when a `SYSCALL` instruction is executed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RETSC", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The following pseudo-instruction is defined to return to this address easily:

Usage: `RETS`

Description: Return from a system call to the address in `RETSC`.

Meaning:
```
JMP ALWAYS RETSC
```

### Interrupt Extension

The Interrupt Extension adds support for basic asynchronous, non-deterministic exceptions. While the
synchronous exceptions in the System Call Extension come from code being executed by the processor,
interrupts are triggered externally to allow the processor to keep time, communicate with
peripherals, and more.

#### Triggering Interrupts
MISA processors supporting the interrupt extension MUST designate one pin as the interrupt pin. The
interrupt pin MAY be active-high or active-low. The interrupt pin is set to its active state to
trigger an interrupt -- the rising or falling edge of the pin MUST cause the processor to finish
executing the current instruction and then set the program counter to the interrupt handler address
at `0xFFF8 - 0xFFF9`.

When this happens, interrupts MUST be automatically disabled by the processor. If the interrupt pin
is toggled, another interrupt MUST not be detected. Taking interrupts does not affect the `CAUSE`
register like system calls or faults.

#### Interrupt Queue
Information about which interrupt was triggered SHOULD be provided to the processor through a
memory-mapped queue. The queue MAY be located anywhere in memory.

The queue SHOULD be structured as follows:

| Bytes | Purpose |
|-------|---------------------|
| 0 | Length |
| 1 | Pop signal |
| 2 | Pop acknowledgement |
| 3 | Interrupt number |
| 4-5 | Argument pointer |

Every field except for the pop signal MUST only be read by the processor. Writing to other fields is
undefined behavior.

The length field defines the number of outstanding interrupts. The interrupt handler SHOULD respond
to every interrupt in the queue before returning, as it is not guaranteed that the interrupt source
will reassert the interrupt pin. If the queue is not emptied before returning, interrupts will be
left unaddressed until the next time the pin is asserted.

When responding to an interrupt, the interrupt handler should read the number and argument pointer
fields, and then pop the entry using the pop handshake.

The pop handshake uses the pop signal and pop acknowledgement fields as request and acknowledge
signals. The pop signal is written by the processor to any non-zero value when the current interrupt
should be popped from the queue. The pop acknowledgement is written by the external hardware to any
non-zero value when the requested pop is completed and the queue fields are updated. Both fields are
zero in the idle state, including after reset and when the Interrupt Extension is first enabled.

The handshake proceeds in four phases. To pop an entry, the processor MUST:

1. Write a non-zero value to the pop signal to request the pop.
2. Wait until the pop acknowledgement is non-zero.
3. Write zero to the pop signal to withdraw the request.
4. Wait until the pop acknowledgement is zero before beginning another pop.

In response, the external hardware must:

1. On the pop signal becoming non-zero, remove the head entry, update the length and (if the queue
   is not empty) the number and argument pointer fields to reflect the new head, and only then write
   a non-zero value to the pop acknowledgement.
2. On the pop signal returning to zero, write zero to the pop acknowledgement.

While the handshake is idle (both the pop signal and pop acknowledgement are zero) and the length is
non-zero, the number and argument pointer fields MUST hold the head entry. To preserve this, the
external hardware MUST modify those fields only during a pop (between observing the pop signal
non-zero and asserting the pop acknowledgement) or, when enqueuing into an empty queue, before
incrementing the length. The processor MUST read those fields only while the handshake is idle and
the length is non-zero.

The exact use of the interrupt number and argument pointer fields are implementation-defined. The
intent is for the interrupt handler to dispatch to a specific service routine based on the number,
passing the argument pointer as a pointer to a particular type of structure containing information
for the service routine. When the length of the queue is zero, the values of the interrupt number
and argument pointer are undefined.

#### Calling Conventions
Because interrupts are not necessarily triggered by the running code in the way system calls are,
the entire processor state MUST be considered to be callee-saved in an interrupt context. The
interrupt handler is responsible for saving and restoring every special and general purpose register
that it modifies.

Three exceptions are the `RSCRATCH0` and `RSCRATCH1` general-purpose registers, and the `FLAGS`
special register. These registers MUST be automatically saved by the processor when an interrupt is
triggered and automatically restored when returning from the interrupt. On entry, `RSCRATCH` is
therefore the only register the handler can freely use before saving anything.

#### Returning From Interrupts
To return from interrupts, the `RETIR` special register is defined, which stores the return address
when an interrupt is triggered.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RETIR", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The following pseudo-instruction is defined to return to this address easily:

Usage: `RETI`

Description: Return from an interrupt to the address in `RETIR`.

Meaning:
```
JMP ALWAYS RETIR
```

When the processor executes `JMP ALWAYS RETIR`, it MUST also perform the following actions
atomically:

1. Restore `RSCRATCH0`, `RSCRATCH1`, `FLAGS`, and `PRIVS.R` (under the Privilege Extension)
2. Set the program counter to the address in `RETIR`
3. Leave the interrupt context and reenable interrupts

Software MUST not return from an interrupt via `RSR RETIR RSCRATCH; JMP ALWAYS RSCRATCH`, as this is
not guaranteed to complete steps 1 and 3.

#### Masking Interrupts
Interrupt masking MUST not be controlled by software. If the Interrupt Extension is supported,
interrupts can always be triggered. Only two conditions prevent the processor from taking new
interrupts:

1. Disabling the Interrupt Extension through the Dynamic Hardware Extension.
2. Being in an interrupt context.

The processor is canonically in an interrupt context under the following formal definition:

- The processor enters an interrupt context when the program counter is set to the address of the
  interrupt handler as a result of the interrupt pin going active
- The processor leaves an interrupt context when a `JMP ALWAYS RETIR` instruction is executed
- Every instruction executed between entering and leaving the interrupt context exists within the
  interrupt context

Software MAY choose to ignore the interrupt by returning immediately from the interrupt handler.

#### System Calls in Interrupts
While the processor is in an interrupt context, system calls SHOULD not be executed. If a system
call is performed in an interrupt context, the processor MUST fault with the reason "Control event"
and the type "Improper system call".

#### Canonical Interrupt Handler
With `RSCRATCH` and `FLAGS` saved by the processor, interrupt handlers are free to modify them. One
method of saving and restoring the full context in the interrupt handler is as follows:

```asm
Interrupt_Handler:
    PUSH2 RAB
    PUSH2 RCD
    ...                         ; Save other general purpose registers

    RSR RADDR RAB
    PUSH2 RAB
    ...                         ; Save other special registers

    ;; Read the interrupt queue, dispatch a service routine, drain the queue

    ...                         ; Restore other special registers
    POP2 RAB
    WSR RADDR RAB

    ...                         ; Restore other general purpose registers
    POP2 RCD
    POP2 RAB

    RETI                        ; Return from the interrupt
```

### Privilege Extension

The Privilege Extension segments the capabilities of the processor into two distinct levels of
privilege, which MAY be used to limit the actions taken by untrusted software.

Machine Mode grants access to all functionality of the processor, and is similar in scope to the
core architecture without the Privilege Extension. User Mode restricts access to certain features of
the core architecture, and provides a way to manage memory I/O at a more cautious level of
privilege.

#### `PRIVS`
Privilege is tracked and controlled using the `PRIVS` special register, which is defined as part of
the Privilege Extension. It is a flags register with the following fields:

| Flag | Bit | Commentary |
|------|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `R` | 0 | The privilege ring bit. 0 for Machine Mode, 1 for User Mode. |

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "R", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "Reserved (optional)", "bits": 15}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

#### User Mode Restrictions

When the processor is in User Mode, the following actions MUST cause a privilege-related fault:

- Execution of `HALT`
- Execution of `RSR` except on `SADDR`, `RADDR`, `FLAGS`, and `PRIVS`
- Execution of `WSR` except on `SADDR`, `RADDR`, and `FLAGS`
- Access to privileged memory, if a memory protection unit is used to manage access based on the
  ring bit

If a privilege error is detected, the processor MUST preempt the instruction which caused the error,
discard any partial result of the instruction, and jump to the fault handler. The `CAUSE` special
register MUST be set to indicate the privilege error for the instruction use or memory access.

#### Points of Privilege Change

Under normal operation, the processor is expected to change privilege modes when the following
occur:

- When any fault occurs which requires the processor to jump to the fault handler (including an User
  Mode privilege error), the processor must first set `PRIVS.R` to 0.
- Under the System Call Extension, when the `SYSCALL` instruction is executed and the exception bit
  is 1, `PRIVS.R` must be set to 0 before the system call handler is entered.
- Under the System Call Extension, when the processor is returned from a system call context, the
  `PRIVS.R` bit must be restored to its initial value before the `SYSCALL`.
- Under the Interrupt Extension, when an interrupt is taken, `PRIVS.R` must be set to 0 before the
  interrupt handler is entered.
- Under the Interrupt Extension, when the processor is returned from an interrupt context, the
  `PRIVS.R` bit must be restored to its initial value before the interrupt occurred. Note that
  interrupts may trigger while the processor is in a system call context, in which case returning
  from the interrupt and returning from the system call will restore different ring bit values.
- When `WSR` is executed on the `PRIVS` special register from Machine Mode, the updated ring bit
  must take effect for the next instruction.

All privilege changes MUST be performed automatically by the processor when an appropriate condition
is detected, except for direct writes to `PRIVS` via `WSR` from Machine Mode.
